description_ru: Эссе о том, почему умение скучать полезно для творчества и самопознания и что мы теряем, заполняя каждую паузу экраном.
text:
Last month I stood in a queue at the post office for eleven minutes, and I did something I had not done in years: I did nothing. I did not check my phone, I did not listen to a podcast and I did not pretend to read a leaflet about parcel insurance. I simply stood there, looking at the ceiling tiles and the flickering strip light, and allowed my mind to wander wherever it wished. Within about three minutes I was restless. Within six I was almost annoyed. By the ninth, something curious had occurred: I had remembered an old argument with my brother, understood why it had gone so badly and drafted, in my head, the first line of an apology.

I report this small episode because I have come to believe that boredom, the much-maligned feeling that we now treat as a malfunction to be repaired as quickly as possible, is one of the most valuable experiences available to a human being, and that we are systematically abolishing it. Never before in history has it been so easy to avoid. A device in every pocket offers an endless supply of novelty, and we reach for it at the faintest hint of an empty moment: on the bus, at the kerb, even in the bathroom. We have, in effect, eliminated the gaps in our day, and I suspect we have eliminated something precious along with them.

Consider what boredom actually is. Psychologists describe it as the unpleasant state of wanting to engage in satisfying activity and being unable to do so. It is, in other words, a form of hunger, and like hunger it exists for a reason. It tells us that our current circumstances are failing to meet some need, and it pushes us to look for something better. A child who complains that there is nothing to do is not defective; she is exercising the very faculty that will later make her a writer, an engineer or a pest-control expert with a rich private life. Parents who rescue their children from every dull afternoon with a tablet are, with the kindest intentions, removing the grindstone on which imagination is sharpened.

There is, moreover, a body of evidence suggesting that idle minds are rather less idle than they appear. When we stop concentrating on a task, a network of brain regions becomes active that scientists call, with admirable bluntness, the default mode network. It appears to be involved in imagining the future, recalling the past and considering other people's perspectives. Several experiments have found that participants who perform a tedious task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently produce more inventive answers to creative problems than those who were given something stimulating. Boredom, it seems, is not the absence of thought but an invitation to a different kind of thought.

The great creators seem to have understood this instinctively. Many writers describe their best ideas arriving in the shower, on a long walk or in the moments before sleep, precisely when their attention was unoccupied. Charles Darwin devoted an hour or so each day to pacing a gravel path behind his house, which he called his thinking path. I doubt that he carried a smartphone, and I am confident that his theory of evolution did not suffer for it.

Of course, I can already hear the objections. It is surely snobbish, someone will say, to romanticise tedium from the comfort of a middle-class life. Boredom is not a pleasure for the person trapped in a monotonous job or a hospital waiting room, and for people in difficult circumstances, a distraction may be a mercy and not a vice. I accept this entirely. There is a difference between the restless, chosen emptiness I am defending and the grinding boredom of those with no autonomy, and it would be a kind of intellectual cruelty to confuse the two. My argument concerns the ordinary person who could stand quietly for a few minutes but has lost the habit.

Others will argue that technology has merely changed the form of our mental life, and that scrolling through the internet is also a way of exploring ideas. There is something to this. A curious person can learn astonishing things in an evening online. But the quality of attention matters, and the typical feed is designed to prevent exactly the sort of drifting that I am recommending. Every few seconds it offers a new stimulus, calibrated to hold us, and we are rarely left alone with a single thought long enough to follow it somewhere unexpected. We consume ideas the way we consume snacks, and we should not be surprised when we feel strangely undernourished.

What, then, should be done? I would not propose anything as drastic as a digital detox, a term that always strikes me as faintly sanctimonious. I would suggest, rather, that we protect a few deliberate pockets of emptiness: the commute without headphones, the lunch break without a screen, the first ten minutes of the morning before the world's demands arrive. At first these gaps will feel uncomfortable, even faintly alarming, much as a muscle protests when it is first used after a long idleness. Persist, and the discomfort fades into something closer to curiosity.

I do not claim that boredom will make anyone a genius. Most of the thoughts that surface in a queue are mundane: a shopping list, an unanswered email, a half-remembered tune. But now and then the mind, left to its own devices, will stitch together two unrelated notions and produce something new, and no algorithm can do that on our behalf. The ability to sit with oneself, unentertained, is not a luxury; it is the basis of self-knowledge.

So the next time you find yourself with a spare minute, I urge you to resist the reflex. Leave the phone in your pocket. Let the strip light flicker. Be bored, deliberately and without apology, and see what you find when nobody is entertaining you. You may discover that the most interesting person in the room was waiting for you to stop talking over them all along.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Безударный слог редуцируется до короткого нейтрального звука: aBOUT, mOment. Не произносите гласные полностью.
Один носовой звук на задней части языка; не добавляйте отдельное г.
Кончик языка слегка между зубами, звук без голоса: thought, something.
imaginAtion, psyCHOlogists: ударение смещается вправо, ближе к концу слова.

questions.question: What happened to the writer during eleven minutes in a queue?
questions.answer: He remembered an argument with his brother and thought of an apology.

questions.question: What is the default mode network?
questions.answer: A network of brain regions active when we are not concentrating on a task.

questions.question: What did Charles Darwin do each day?
questions.answer: He walked on his thinking path.

questions.question: What does the writer recommend instead of a digital detox?
questions.answer: Protecting a few deliberate pockets of emptiness in the day.
